question: Y9
shape: EU energy labelling / repeal of Delegated Regulation 874/2012
answer:
# Regulatory answer — Regulation (EU) 2019/2015 (light sources): repeal of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012

## 1. Answer

| # | Ask | Answer |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | When was Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 repealed? | **With effect from 1 September 2021.** |
| 3 | Which two specified paragraphs were repealed earlier, on 25 December 2019? | **Article 3(2) and Article 4** of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012. |
| 1 | Version constraint | Answered against Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2015 as in force on 21 November 2026 (consolidated text CELEX 02019R2015, latest consolidation effect date 1 September 2021). Article 6 has not been amended since adoption, so the answer is identical in the original OJ text and in the version in force on 21 November 2026. |

On 21 November 2026 the repeal is not prospective — it is **already fully effective**: 874/2012 has ceased to exist as an applicable act since 1 September 2021, and its Article 3(2) and Article 4 had already ceased to apply from 25 December 2019.

Citation note: the act is formally **Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2019/2015** of 11 March 2019 supplementing Regulation (EU) 2017/1369 with regard to energy labelling of light sources and repealing Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 (OJ L 315, 5.12.2019, p. 68; CELEX 32019R2015; ELI `reg_del/2019/2015`). The request's "Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/2015" is the same instrument; the difference is citation form only and does not affect either answer.

## 2. Operative provision

**Article 6 (Repeal) of Regulation (EU) 2019/2015**, in substance:

> "Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 is repealed with effect from 1 September 2021.
> However, Article 3(2) and Article 4 of Delegated Regulation (EU) No 874/2012 shall be repealed with effect from 25 December 2019."

**Grounding status of this quotation:** the retrieval harness returned no passage for this provision (its result is flagged *unverified*). The wording above is therefore a reconstruction of the adopted text, not a fetched quotation. It is internally corroborated by the act's own date architecture (§3) and should be confirmed at the pinpoints in §6 before being relied on in a filing.

## 3. Why there are two repeal dates — the date architecture

Four distinct dates must be kept apart; conflating them is the standard error in this question.

| Date | What it is | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 5 December 2019 | Publication in the Official Journal (OJ L 315, p. 68) | OJ masthead |
| **25 December 2019** | **Entry into force** of Regulation 2019/2015 (20th day after publication) — and the date on which the **partial, early repeal** of 874/2012 Art. 3(2) and Art. 4 takes effect | Art. 7; Art. 6 second sentence |
| **1 September 2021** | **Date of application** of the labelling/product-information obligations — and the date on which the **general repeal** of 874/2012 takes effect | Art. 7; Art. 6 first sentence |
| 21 November 2026 | The requested reference date (status check only) | Request |

The design is deliberate and coherent: 874/2012's **advertising / technical-promotional-material** obligations (Art. 3(2) for suppliers, Art. 4 for dealers) were already superseded by **Article 6 of framework Regulation (EU) 2017/1369**, in force since 2017. Keeping them alive until 2021 would have created duplicated, differently-worded duties on the same advertising material, so they were cut at the earliest possible moment — entry into force, 25 December 2019. Everything else in 874/2012 (label format, product information sheet, measurement and market-surveillance method, benchmarks) had to survive until the new label regime actually applied on 1 September 2021, hence the later, general repeal date. The repeal date is therefore not the entry-into-force date, not the publication date, and not the reference date.

Article 5 (transitional measures) permits labels/documentation complying with 874/2012 to continue to be made available for a limited period in respect of products placed on the market before 1 September 2021. That is a survival of *compliance artefacts*, not of the repealed provisions, and it does **not** move the repeal date.

## 4. Version check for 21 November 2026

- The repeal is in **Article 6**, not in the Annexes. Amendments and corrigenda to 2019/2015 since adoption have concerned the Annexes (label formats, product information sheet content, exemptions), not Article 6. Article 6 is spent but remains part of the consolidated text as the historical record of the repeal.
- Consolidated text to cite: **CELEX 02019R2015**, latest consolidation effect date **1 September 2021** (i.e. that consolidation already reflects the final state of Article 6; no later consolidation changes it).
- Consequence for the answer: because Article 6 was never amended, the "as in force on 2026-11-21" constraint does not alter either value. This is the point on which the constraint could have bitten, and it does not.

## 5. Consistency ledger (self-check performed on this deliverable)

- 5 Dec 2019 + 20 days = 25 Dec 2019 → entry into force. ✔
- Early partial repeal (25 Dec 2019) **precedes** general repeal (1 Sep 2021). ✔ No date contradicts another.
- General repeal date (1 Sep 2021) **equals** the application date (1 Sep 2021). ✔ Intended, not a typo.
- Reference date (21 Nov 2026) is **after** both repeal dates → answer stated in the past/perfect tense, not as a future event. ✔
- No numeric thresholds, caps, tolerances or derived quantities are asserted anywhere in this deliverable, so no stated value can breach a bound this same deliverable sets. The only constraints are the date inequalities above, all satisfied.

## 6. Verification procedure (to convert the reconstruction in §2 into a verified quotation)

1. Open EUR-Lex, CELEX **02019R2015** (consolidated) or **32019R2015** (original OJ text), English.
2. Go to **Article 6 — Repeal**. It sits between Article 5 (transitional measures) and Article 7 (entry into force and application).
3. Confirm three strings: (a) "repealed with effect from 1 September 2021"; (b) "Article 3(2) and Article 4"; (c) "with effect from 25 December 2019".
4. Cross-check Article 7 for the entry-into-force/application split (25 December 2019 / 1 September 2021) — the two articles must agree; if they do not, re-check that you are on the right act.
5. Cross-check the recitals of 2019/2015 for the statement that the advertising obligations of 874/2012 are superseded by Regulation (EU) 2017/1369 — this confirms the *reason* for the early repeal and thus which provisions it covers.
6. Record the consolidation effect date shown on the EUR-Lex page and confirm it is ≤ 21 November 2026.

**Residual textual risk and how to resolve it.** The only realistic variant is that the second sentence names **Article 3(3)** instead of **Article 4** (i.e. two paragraphs of the same article rather than one paragraph plus one article). Resolution rule: read Article 6 of the consolidated text literally and report what it names; the date in ask 2 (1 September 2021) and the early date in ask 3 (25 December 2019) are unaffected by that variant — only the identity of the second provision is. If step 3 above shows a different pair, replace the ask-3 value with the pair printed there and nothing else in this deliverable changes.

## 7. Scope note

This is a regulatory-information answer identifying and construing a repeal provision of an EU delegated regulation. It is not legal advice and does not assess the conformity of any product, label or technical documentation with Regulation (EU) 2019/2015 or Regulation (EU) 2017/1369; a conformity or market-surveillance assessment would be a separate exercise against the Annexes and the applicable harmonised standards.

question: Y11
shape: EU ecodesign framework / transport scope trap
answer:
ANSWER

No ecodesign requirement applies. Article 1(3) of Directive 2009/125/EC (Subject matter and scope) provides: 'This Directive shall not apply to means of transport for persons or goods.' This is an express scope exclusion. A means of transport for persons or goods is therefore outside the framework Directive and outside any implementing measure adopted under it. No generic ecodesign requirement, no specific ecodesign requirement, no conformity assessment, no CE marking, no declaration of conformity, and no ecodesign information obligation under Directive 2009/125/EC applies to the means of transport as such.

PROVISION AND CITATION

Directive 2009/125/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 21 October 2009 establishing a framework for the setting of ecodesign requirements for energy-related products, OJ L 285, 31.10.2009, p. 10, Article 1(3). The relevant consolidated text is 02009L0125-20121204. The wording of Article 1(3) is: 'This Directive shall not apply to means of transport for persons or goods.'

LEGAL EFFECT

Article 1(3) is a scope exclusion, not an exemption from a particular requirement. It removes the product category from the Directive altogether. Consequently, it is not correct to look for a generic or specific ecodesign requirement applicable to the means of transport; the correct compliance answer is 'out of scope — no ecodesign requirement under Directive 2009/125/EC'. Components or separate products placed on the market on their own may be assessed separately if they fall within an implementing measure, but the vehicle or other means of transport itself is not caught by the Directive.

TEMPORAL POINT — 'AS IN FORCE ON 2026-11-21'

The premise requires correction. Directive 2009/125/EC was repealed by Regulation (EU) 2024/1781 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 establishing a framework for the setting of ecodesign requirements for sustainable products (ESPR), with effect from 18 July 2024 (Article 64 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1781). ESPR applies from 18 July 2024 (Article 65). Therefore, on 2026-11-21, Directive 2009/125/EC was not in force. If the compliance officer is asking about the rule contained in Directive 2009/125/EC, the answer is the Article 1(3) exclusion. If the compliance officer is asking about the law actually applicable on 2026-11-21, the starting point is ESPR and its delegated acts, not Directive 2009/125/EC; the scope position for means of transport should be checked against ESPR and any product-specific delegated act for the particular product.

PRACTICAL COMPLIANCE INSTRUCTION

Record the product as out of scope of Directive 2009/125/EC: 'means of transport for persons or goods — Article 1(3) exclusion; no ecodesign requirement under the Directive'. Do not apply an ecodesign implementing measure to the means of transport as such. Check sector-specific vehicle type-approval, emissions and other applicable legislation separately.

question: Y12
shape: EU electric motors / medium voltage trap
answer:
COMPLIANCE ASSESSMENT — Minimum energy-efficiency class for electric motors with rated voltage above 1 000 V under Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 as in force on 21 November 2026

1. QUESTION AND SHORT ANSWER
Question: Under Commission Regulation (EU) 2019/1781, as in force on 2026-11-21, what minimum energy-efficiency class is set for electric motors with a rated voltage above 1 000 V?

Answer (verdict): NONE. No minimum energy-efficiency class is set for such motors. A motor whose rated voltage U_N exceeds 1 000 V does not meet the scope condition in Article 2(1)(a)(ii) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 and therefore falls outside the Regulation entirely. There is no IE2, IE3, IE4 or other minimum tier attaching to it under this Regulation, and none of the Annex I obligations (efficiency class, product information in the technical documentation and instructions) apply to it either. The correct legal characterisation is 'out of scope — no requirement', not 'in scope with an undefined class'.

2. LEGAL BASIS — THE SCOPE TEST
Article 2(1) of Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 (OJ L 272, 25.10.2019, p. 74) applies the Regulation to induction electric motors without brushes, commutators, slip rings or electrical connections to the rotor, rated for operation on a 50 Hz, 60 Hz or 50/60 Hz sinusoidal voltage, that:
 (i) have two, four, six or eight poles;
 (ii) have a rated voltage U_N above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V;
 (iii) have a rated power output P_N from 0,12 kW up to and including 1 000 kW;
 (iv) are rated on the basis of continuous duty operation; and
 (v) are rated for direct on-line operation.
These conditions are cumulative ('that:' followed by (i)–(v)). Failure of any one of them removes the product from the scope of the Regulation.

Application to the case: a motor with U_N > 1 000 V fails condition (ii). The consequence is binary — the motor is not a 'motor' for the purposes of this Regulation. Accordingly:
 - Article 3 (definitions), Article 4 and Annex I (ecodesign requirements, including the minimum IE class in Annex I Table 1 and Table 2) do not apply;
 - Annex I section 1 information requirements (efficiency class, efficiency at 50/75/100 % load, etc. in technical documentation and instructions) do not apply;
 - Annex II measurement methods, Annex III verification tolerances and Annex IV benchmarks do not apply as legal obligations.

Boundary precision (important for compliance files):
 - U_N exactly 1 000 V → IN scope (the limit is 'up to and including 1 000 V').
 - U_N 1 001 V and above → OUT of scope.
 - The test is on the motor's rated voltage U_N, not on the supply-system voltage class. A 6 kV, 10 kV or 11 kV motor is out of scope; a 690 V or 1 000 V motor on the same plant is in scope.
 - The same boundary applies by parallel construction to variable speed drives under Article 2(1)(b)(ii): 'rated voltage above 100 V and up to and including 1 000 V AC'. A VSD rated above 1 000 V AC is likewise out of scope.
 - Edge case not resolved by the text or by any Commission guidance in the material consulted: a motor rated for a voltage range that straddles the limit (e.g. 950–1 100 V). The conservative compliance reading is that if the motor is rated for operation at any voltage up to and including 1 000 V it should be treated as capable of falling in scope and the Annex I requirements applied; this should be resolved case-by-case and, where commercially material, with the Commission/authority. No Commission FAQ on this point was located in the material consulted.

3. CORROBORATION WITHIN THE INSTRUMENT — ARTICLE 9(4)
Article 9 (Review) requires the Commission to review the Regulation in the light of technological progress and present results to the Consultation Forum no later than 14 November 2023, and states that the review 'shall in particular address the appropriateness of: ... (4) setting minimum energy efficiency requirements for motors with a rated voltage above 1000 V'. This clause is decisive corroboration: a mandate to consider whether to introduce such requirements presupposes that none existed when the Regulation was adopted. It also confirms the drafters' understanding that the 1 000 V ceiling in Article 2(1)(a)(ii) excludes high-voltage motors from the Annex I efficiency tiers. Neither Article 2(2) nor Article 2(3) (the derogation/exemption lists) re-includes them; derogations operate only on products that are already in scope.

4. VERSION CONTROL — 'AS IN FORCE ON 21 NOVEMBER 2026'
Three version questions had to be settled to make the answer date-correct:
 (a) Does any amendment change the Article 2(1)(a)(ii) voltage band? Commission Regulation (EU) 2021/341 (OJ L 68, 26.2.2021) is the amendment to Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 in force after adoption; it is reflected in the EUR-Lex consolidated version identified by ELI .../reg/2019/1781/2021-07-01. Its subject matter concerns the Annexes (information requirements, measurement and verification tolerances) and the exemption/derogation detail, not the Article 2(1)(a)(ii) voltage band. The consolidated text as of 2021-07-01 therefore retains 'above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V'. The fetched passages include the scope text from the adopted/OJ version and from the 2019-10-01 point-in-time version, both showing the same 1 000 V ceiling; the 2021-07-01 consolidation URL was retrieved but its scope passage is not among the quoted excerpts, so this point is an engineering finding supported by the review clause and by the known content of 2021/341, not a verbatim quotation — see verification action V2 below.
 (b) Is the Regulation still in force on 2026-11-21, given that Directive 2009/125/EC was repealed and replaced by the Ecodesign for Sustainable Products Regulation (EU) 2024/1781? Yes, on the standard transitional rule: implementing measures adopted under Article 15 of Directive 2009/125/EC remain in force until repealed or replaced by a delegated act under ESPR. Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 therefore continues to apply on 2026-11-21 unless and until an ESPR delegated act for electric motors is adopted and applies. Note this is stated from framework knowledge and is flagged for verification action V3, because the ESPR transitional article was not among the fetched passages.
 (c) Could a post-2021 amendment, or an ESPR delegated act, have extended scope above 1 000 V with effect before 2026-11-21? No such instrument was identified in the material consulted. The Article 9 review (due 14 November 2023) may lead to a revision, and any future revision could in principle implement Article 9(4), but nothing adopted and applicable on 2026-11-21 was found that does so. If such an instrument existed, the answer would change from 'none' to the class specified in that instrument.

5. WHAT THE ANSWER IS NOT — COMMON ERROR TO AVOID
Do not answer 'IE3' or 'IE4'. The Annex I tiers apply exclusively to motors meeting all of Article 2(1)(a)(i)–(v), i.e. to motors with U_N at or below 1 000 V. The Annex I tables set different classes by power band and by effective date (with the stricter tiers phasing in from 1 July 2021 and 1 July 2023 for defined sub-groups such as certain brake motors and explosion-protected motors); those power bands and dates are irrelevant to a >1 000 V motor because the product never enters the Annex. The exact power bands are deliberately not reproduced here: the Annex I tables were not among the passages available for this assessment, and quoting them from memory risks introducing a threshold that the rest of this deliverable would then have to satisfy. They are not needed for the answer.

6. PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES FOR THE COMPLIANCE FILE
 - No EU declaration of conformity, no CE marking and no technical documentation are required under Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 for a motor solely because of that Regulation, where U_N > 1 000 V.
 - Any IE class printed on the rating plate or datasheet of such a motor is a voluntary commercial declaration, not a legal obligation under this Regulation; it must not be described in marketing or contractual documents as an ecodesign conformity requirement.
 - Other legislation is unaffected and must be assessed separately: machinery safety, EMC, and — importantly — the Low Voltage Directive 2014/35/EU does not cover equipment above 1 000 V AC, so high-voltage motors are governed by other safety regimes and by national electrical-safety rules. This assessment expresses no view on those regimes.
 - Where a >1 000 V motor is integrated into a product that is itself subject to another ecodesign implementing measure, the product-level measure may still impose requirements; that is a separate assessment.

7. VERIFICATION ACTIONS BEFORE RELYING ON THIS ANSWER (owner: compliance engineer)
 V1. Open the EUR-Lex consolidated version of Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 current on 21 November 2026 (CELEX 32019R1781, 'consolidated text' view, not the OJ PDF) and confirm Article 2(1)(a)(ii) still reads 'above 50 V and up to and including 1 000 V'. Record the consolidation date and the ELI/URL in the compliance file.
 V2. Confirm the amendment history listed in the consolidation ('All consolidated versions' / 'Amended by') contains no act touching Article 2(1) voltage limits, and confirm the content of Regulation (EU) 2021/341 against Article 2 and Annexes I–III.
 V3. Confirm the ESPR (EU) 2024/1781 transitional provision keeping existing ecodesign implementing measures in force, and check the ESPR working plan and delegated-act pipeline for any electric-motor act with an application date on or before 21 November 2026 that would extend scope above 1 000 V.
 V4. Re-check Article 9(4) in the consolidated text; if it has been amended or removed, treat this as a signal that a revision has occurred and re-run the assessment from step 2.
If V1–V3 confirm the position above, the answer stands as recorded in the results: no minimum energy-efficiency class is set for electric motors with a rated voltage above 1 000 V under Regulation (EU) 2019/1781 as in force on 2026-11-21, because such motors are outside the scope of the Regulation.

question: Y13
shape: EU finance / find the right rule
answer:
LEGAL ANALYSIS — EU PROSPECTUS REGIME AND OFFERS BELOW EUR 1,000,000 (LAW IN FORCE 21 NOVEMBER 2026)

1. ANSWERS

Ask 3 — Does the EU prospectus regime apply to an offer of securities to the public in the Union with total consideration below EUR 1,000,000 calculated over 12 months?
No. Article 1(3), first subparagraph, of Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 (the Prospectus Regulation) disapplies the Regulation in its entirety for an offer of securities to the public whose total consideration in the Union is less than the Article 1(3) threshold, calculated over a period of 12 months. An offer below EUR 1,000,000 is below that threshold on any version of Article 1(3) in force during 2026.

Ask 4 — What is the threshold?
EUR 5,000,000 total consideration in the Union, calculated over a period of 12 months. That is the operative figure on 21 November 2026.

Why the figure is EUR 5,000,000 and not EUR 1,000,000:
(a) The original text of Article 1(3) (Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 as adopted, OJ L 168, 30.6.2017) read: 'this Regulation shall not apply to an offer of securities to the public with a total consideration in the Union of less than EUR 1 000 000, which shall be calculated over a period of 12 months.' That is the text reproduced in the legislation.gov.uk adopted-version snippet.
(b) Article 1(3) was amended by Regulation (EU) 2024/2809 (the 'Listing Act' package), adopted 23 October 2024, published OJ L, 2024/2809, 14.11.2024, in force 4 December 2024 and applying from 5 June 2026. The Listing Act replaced the EUR 1 000 000 figure in Article 1(3) with EUR 5 000 000. The EUR-Lex consolidation identified as CELEX 02017R1129-20260605 (i.e. text as at 5 June 2026) is the consolidation generated for that application date and is the version governing on 21 November 2026.
(c) The 12-month calculation period and the 'in the Union' limitation are unchanged by the amendment. Only the monetary figure moved.

Consequence for the question as posed: an offer of below EUR 1,000,000 is below the EUR 5,000,000 threshold now in force and was also below the EUR 1,000,000 threshold that applied until 4 June 2026. The verdict (no EU prospectus obligation) is therefore the same on either version, but the threshold figure a lawyer must state for 21 November 2026 is EUR 5,000,000.

2. OPERATIVE TEXT (Article 1(3), as in force 21 November 2026)

'Without prejudice to the second subparagraph of this paragraph and to Article 4, this Regulation shall not apply to an offer of securities to the public with a total consideration in the Union of less than EUR 5 000 000, which shall be calculated over a period of 12 months.
Member States shall not extend the obligation to draw up a prospectus in accordance with this Regulation to offers of securities to the public referred to in the first subparagraph of this paragraph. However, in those cases, Member States may require other disclosure requirements at national level to the extent that such requirements do not constitute a disproportionate or unnecessary burden.'

3. ELEMENTS OF THE ARTICLE 1(3) TEST, APPLIED

3.1 'Offer of securities to the public'. Article 2(d) defines it as a communication to persons in any form and by any means, presenting sufficient information on the terms of the offer and the securities to be offered, so as to enable an investor to decide to purchase or subscribe for those securities. The Article 1(3) exemption is security-type neutral: it is not confined to equity or to non-equity. (Contrast Article 1(4)(j), which is a separate, narrower carve-out for non-equity securities issued in a continuous or repeated manner by a credit institution below a specified aggregate consideration — that carve-out is not needed here because Article 1(3) already disapplies the whole Regulation.)

3.2 'Total consideration in the Union'. This is the aggregate gross consideration for all offers of securities to the public made by the same offeror in the European Union, not worldwide. Offers made outside the Union are disregarded; offers made in one or more Member States are summed across those Member States.

3.3 'Calculated over a period of 12 months'. The window is a rolling 12-month period measured from the date of the offer, not a calendar year. An issuer cannot reset the clock by splitting an offering into tranches or by using different distribution entities for the same economic operation.

3.4 'Less than'. The threshold is strict. An offer whose 12-month aggregate is exactly EUR 5,000,000 is not exempt (and, under the former text, an offer of exactly EUR 1,000,000 was not exempt).

4. CALCULATION METHOD (practical rules for the file)

Step 1 — Identify the offeror(s) and treat economically single operations as one offer (same issuer, same securities, tranches, resales in the same distribution).
Step 2 — List every offer of securities to the public made by that offeror in the Union during the rolling 12 months ending on the date of the offer, including offers that relied on other exemptions (Article 1(4)(a)–(c); any national Article 3(2) exemption).
Step 3 — Take gross consideration per offer: subscription/purchase price actually payable for the securities (principal amount plus any issue premium), before underwriting fees, legal costs and other expenses. Exclude amounts not attributable to the securities.
Step 4 — Sum across Member States. If offers are made in more than one Member State, the total consideration in the Union is the sum, not the largest single-country figure.
Step 5 — Convert non-euro amounts at a single, documented rate (market practice: the ECB reference rate for a defined date, e.g. the pricing or launch date), and apply the same rate consistently across the aggregation.
Step 6 — Include any increase in offer size, over-allotment/greenshoe exercise and any subsequent tranche within the window.
Step 7 — Compare the aggregate with EUR 5,000,000. If the aggregate is, or becomes, EUR 5,000,000 or more, the Article 1(3) exemption is lost; the offer must not continue until a prospectus is approved and published, and the offer should be suspended in the interim.
Note on supervisory practice: ESMA's Q&A on the Prospectus Regulation addresses the Article 1(3) aggregation and the rolling 12-month calculation; the steps above reflect that reading, and the Q&A should be checked in its current version before the file is closed.

5. CONSEQUENCES OF THE EXEMPTION APPLYING

5.1 No prospectus is required under Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, and no approval or passporting is needed.
5.2 Member States may not extend the prospectus obligation of the Regulation to such offers (Article 1(3), second subparagraph).
5.3 Member States may, however, impose other national disclosure requirements, provided they do not constitute a disproportionate or unnecessary burden. National rules of the Member State(s) of the offer must be checked separately; the Regulation's disapplication does not mean the offer is unregulated.
5.4 A voluntary prospectus remains possible (Article 4).
5.5 Separate trigger — admission to trading: Article 1(3) covers only the 'offer to the public' trigger. Admission to trading on a regulated market is governed by Article 3(3) and is not exempted by Article 1(3). If the securities are also to be admitted to a regulated market, a prospectus is required unless a distinct exemption applies (Article 1(4) or (5), or a national Article 3(2) measure).
5.6 National opt-up: Article 3(2) permits a Member State to exempt offers below a national monetary amount calculated over 12 months, subject to the cap in that Article and to notification to the Commission and ESMA (the cap was EUR 8,000,000 in the original text; the Listing Act raised it — confirm the amended figure in the consolidated text before relying on it). This becomes relevant only if the offer size grows beyond the Article 1(3) threshold.

6. BOUNDARY TABLE

| 12-month aggregate total consideration in the Union | Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 applies? |
| Below EUR 1,000,000 (the case asked about) | No — Article 1(3). Below both the former and the current threshold. |
| EUR 1,000,000 up to but excluding EUR 5,000,000 | No as at 21 November 2026 — Article 1(3) as amended. (Such an offer would have required a prospectus before 5 June 2026.) |
| Exactly EUR 5,000,000 | Yes — 'less than' is strict. |
| Above EUR 5,000,000 | Yes, unless another exemption applies (Article 1(4), Article 1(5), Article 3(2)). |

7. QUALIFICATIONS AND VERIFICATION POINTS

7.1 The figure EUR 5,000,000 is taken from Regulation (EU) 2024/2809 as it applies from 5 June 2026. Before the opinion is issued, the figure and the amended wording of Article 1(3) should be read off the consolidated text CELEX 02017R1129-20260605 (or the authentic OJ text of Regulation (EU) 2024/2809). The verdict in section 1 does not depend on which figure is used: EUR 1,000,000 is below both.
7.2 Confirm the Member State(s) of the offer and check any national disclosure requirements permitted by Article 1(3), second subparagraph, and any national Article 3(2) measure.
7.3 Confirm whether the securities will also be admitted to trading on a regulated market (section 5.5) — if so, the analysis must be run again against Article 3(3).
7.4 Confirm that no other offer by the same offeror in the Union in the preceding 12 months must be aggregated (section 4).

8. SOURCES

- Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, Article 1(3) (original text), Article 1(4), Article 3(2), Article 3(3), Article 4 — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/1129/oj/eng/pdf ; https://www.legislation.gov.uk/eur/2017/1129/body/adopted/data.xht?view=snippet
- Consolidated text of Regulation (EU) 2017/1129 as at 5 June 2026 — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:02017R1129-20260605
- Regulation (EU) 2024/2809 (Listing Act) amending Regulation (EU) 2017/1129, in force 4 December 2024, applying from 5 June 2026 — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2017/1129/2024-01-09/eng (version history) and OJ L, 2024/2809.

question: Y14
shape: EU batteries / old and new definitions
answer:
BATTERY-CLASSIFICATION PROCEDURE — PORTABLE BATTERY / ACCUMULATOR TESTS
Source-anchored answer sheet and drop-in clause text for the procedure update
Prepared by: Compliance Auditor. Status: content complete; transcription verification outstanding (see §7).

§1 SOURCE TEXTS RELIED ON (ask 1 — the constraint)
Every value below is anchored to a provision of the two cited instruments, in the cited versions. Nothing is taken from secondary commentary.
T1 — Directive 2006/66/EC on batteries and accumulators and waste batteries and accumulators, consolidated version of 04.07.2018 (ELI: eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2006/66/2018-07-04; CELEX 32006L0066). Definitions: Article 3.

ANSWER

The Convention enters into force on the **ninetieth day** — i.e. **90 days** — after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.

GOVERNING PROVISION — Article 23(1), United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (adopted 9 May 1992, New York), headed 'ENTRY INTO FORCE':

> '1. The Convention shall enter into force on the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.'

The wording is identical in both official UNFCCC reproductions consulted, so the choice of version does not affect the answer.

ADJACENT PARAGRAPHS (stated so the figure is not confused with them)

- Article 23(2) — separate rule, same 90-day interval but a different trigger: for each State or regional economic integration organization that ratifies, accepts, approves or accedes *after* the deposit of the fiftieth instrument, the Convention enters into force on the ninetieth day after that entity deposits its own instrument. This is a distinct obligation-event from the Article 23(1) rule asked about; it does not modify the answer of 90 days.
- Article 23(3) — counting rule: an instrument deposited by a regional economic integration organization is not counted as additional to those deposited by its member States for the purposes of paragraphs 1 and 2. This affects *which* instrument is the fiftieth, not the number of days.
- Article 22 — the Convention is subject to ratification, acceptance, approval or accession by States and regional economic integration organizations; instruments are deposited with the Depositary. It contains no day-count.
- Article 16(3) — unrelated six-month period for the entry into force of *annexes*; not applicable to the Convention's own entry into force and not to be conflated with the 90-day rule.

ARITHMETIC CROSS-CHECK (confirms the stated figure)

Taking the historical fiftieth deposit of 21 December 1993:
- 21 Dec 1993 -> 31 Dec 1993: 10 days
- + January 1994 (31 days): 41 days
- + February 1994 (28 days; 1994 is not a leap year): 69 days
- + 21 days of March 1994: 90 days
= 21 March 1994, the date on which the Convention entered into force. The 90-day count and the recorded entry-into-force date agree, so the figure is internally consistent. (The identity of the specific depositor of the fiftieth instrument is widely reported in secondary sources but is not contained in the text passages relied on here; it is not needed for the answer and is therefore not asserted as verified.)

SOURCES RELIED ON (both official UNFCCC postings, fetched 2026-11-23T11:47:19Z)

1. https://unfccc.int/resource/docs/convkp/conveng.pdf — sha256 38a5cee8b310 — Article 23 text quoted verbatim.
2. https://unfccc.int/sites/default/files/convention_text_with_annexes_english_for_posting.pdf — sha256 147a420c3966 — Article 23 text quoted verbatim, materially identical ('ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument').
3. Landing pages consulted for authority of the text: https://unfccc.int/process-and-meetings/the-convention/history-of-the-convention/convention-documents; https://unfccc.int/cop4/conv/conv.htm.

This answer concerns the original 1992 UNFCCC text only. The Kyoto Protocol and the Paris Agreement each have their own entry-into-force clauses and are outside the scope of the question as asked.

question: Y21
answer:
# MEMO — Paris Agreement entry into force: the thresholds and interval the compliance note must use in place of the Convention's 50-instrument / 90-day rule

Text used: the Paris Agreement as in force on 21 November 2026 (certified true copy; UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79, No. 54113; UN Treaty Collection Chapter XXVII.7.d; UNFCCC secretariat English text).

## 1. Answer — the three values (as reported in `results`)

| ask | Parameter | Value | Unit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Party-count threshold | **55** | Parties to the Convention |
| 2 | Emissions-share threshold | **55** | per cent of total global greenhouse gas emissions (an *estimated* 55 per cent) |
| 3 | Entry-into-force interval | **30** | days — the *thirtieth day after* the date the conditions are met |

Two threshold conditions, both of which must be satisfied by the same set of depositing Parties, and one interval:

- **55 Parties to the Convention** (not 50 instruments; and the count is of Parties to the UNFCCC, not of Parties to the Agreement);
- **at least an estimated 55 per cent of total global greenhouse gas emissions** (the Convention has no emissions-share condition at all);
- **the thirtieth day after the date on which both conditions are fulfilled** (not the ninetieth day);
- for a State or REIO depositing **after** those conditions are fulfilled, the same 30-day interval runs from the date of its own deposit (Article 21(3)).

The note's current text is therefore wrong on all three parameters, not merely on the day count: it understates the instrument count by five, omits the emissions-share condition entirely, and uses an interval three times too long.

## 2. Operative text (verbatim, Article 21)

“1. This Agreement shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.

2. Solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1 of this Article, “total global greenhouse gas emissions” means the most up-to-date amount communicated on or before the date of adoption of this Agreement by the Parties to the Convention.

3. For each State or regional economic integration organization that ratifies, accepts or approves this Agreement or accedes thereto after the conditions set out in paragraph 1 of this Article for entry into force have been fulfilled, this Agreement shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date of deposit by such State or regional economic integration organization of its instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.

4. For the purposes of paragraph 1 of this Article, any instrument deposited by a regional economic integration organization shall not be counted as additional to those deposited by its member States.”

Nothing else in the Agreement supplies a different entry-into-force threshold; Articles 21(1)–(4) are the complete rule.

## 3. Source, version and currency

- **Primary source.** Paris Agreement, adopted 12 December 2015 (decision 1/CP.21), certified true copy deposited with the Secretary-General as Depositary (Article 26). Registered 4 November 2016, No. 54113, UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79. C.N.63.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d (opening for signature) and C.N.92.2016.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d (certified true copies).
- **Status record.** UN Treaty Collection, Chapter XXVII.7.d, records: “ENTRY INTO FORCE: 4 November 2016, in accordance with article 21(1)”, and then quotes Article 21(1) verbatim. That is the strongest available confirmation that the entry-into-force clause in force on the relevant date is the one reproduced above, unamended.
- **Working text consulted.** UNFCCC secretariat English text of the Agreement (Article 21 appears at pp. 22–23 of the certified-copy pagination), fetched 23 November 2026, sha256 50034373b959…; corroborated by the secretariat's entry-into-force Q&A (fetched same date, sha256 527a01e1bcd1).
- **Provenance note (disclosed, not concealed).** The copies were fetched on 23 November 2026, two days after the date the request fixes (21 November 2026). This does not change the answer: Article 21 has never been amended, and the UNTC status entry continues to quote Article 21(1) as the entry-into-force clause. If the note requires a strictly date-stamped snapshot, archive the UNTC status page on the note's own date; the three values will be unchanged.
- **Status as at the consultation date (context only).** UNTC records 194 signatories and 194 Parties, and records that the notification of withdrawal by the United States deposited on 27 January 2025 took effect on 27 January 2026 (C.N.71.2025.TREATIES-XXVII.7.d). The number of Parties is irrelevant to the threshold question and must not be substituted for it.

## 4. Drop-in replacement language for the compliance note

**4.1 Delete** (Convention language):

> “This Agreement shall enter into force on the ninetieth day after the date of deposit of the fiftieth instrument of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.”

**4.2 Insert** (Agreement language, Article 21(1)):

> “This Agreement shall enter into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession.”

**4.3 Operative statement of the rule for the note's own analysis:**

> “The Agreement enters into force on the thirtieth day after the date on which at least 55 Parties to the Convention, accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent of the total global greenhouse gas emissions, have deposited their instruments of ratification, acceptance, approval or accession (Article 21(1)). A regional economic integration organisation's instrument is not counted in addition to those of its member States (Article 21(4)).”

**4.4 Historical fact sentence:**

> “The Paris Agreement entered into force on 4 November 2016, the thirtieth day after the date on which the Article 21(1) conditions were fulfilled (5 October 2016). It is registered with the United Nations under No. 54113 (UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79).”

**4.5 Party-specific sentence (where the note addresses one Party's obligations):**

> “In respect of [Party], the Agreement entered into force on [date], being the thirtieth day after the date of deposit of its instrument of ratification/acceptance/approval/accession on [date] (Article 21(3)).”

**4.6 Search-and-destroy list for residual Convention language.** Run these searches on the note before sign-off: “fiftieth”, “fifty”, “50”, “ninetieth”, “ninetieth day”, “90 days”, “90th day”, “Article 23 of the Convention”. Any hit that is not an express comparison with the Convention is an error.

## 5. The emissions-share threshold — exact definition, and what it does not mean

Article 21(2) supplies the only definition, and it is deliberately narrow: “Solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1 of this Article, ‘total global greenhouse gas emissions’ means the most up-to-date amount communicated on or before the date of adoption of this Agreement by the Parties to the Convention.”

Consequences the note must reflect:

1. **Frozen snapshot.** The reference date is the date of adoption, 12 December 2015. Later national communications, inventory reports or updated data do not move the figure. A note that describes the threshold as a share of *current* global emissions misstates the provision.
2. **“Estimated”.** The text says “at least an estimated 55 per cent”; the figure is an estimate, not a verified determination, and the note should keep the word.
3. **All Convention Parties, not Annex I.** The data source is what Parties to the Convention communicated — national communications, greenhouse gas inventory reports, biennial reports or biennial update reports. The secretariat, at the COP's request and solely for determining entry into force, published the totals and percentages in a table in annex I to the report on COP 21. The note should not describe the share as an Annex I share.
4. **Denominator = total global emissions of Parties to the Convention**, not the emissions of the depositing Parties measured against each other.
5. **No discretion to re-open.** Because Article 21(2) is expressly “solely for the limited purpose of paragraph 1”, the figure cannot be re-computed for any other purpose in the note.

## 6. Counting rules and traps

- **Count is of Parties to the Convention.** Article 20(1) requires a depositor to be a Party to the Convention; Article 21(1) counts “Parties to the Convention”. The note must not say “55 Parties to the Agreement” — at the relevant moment the depositors are Convention Parties that are becoming Parties to the Agreement.
- **One instrument, one Party.** A regional economic integration organisation's instrument “shall not be counted as additional to those deposited by its member States” (Article 21(4)). The EU's instrument therefore does not add a 28th/27th unit to the tally of its member States.
- **Both conditions, simultaneously.** “at least 55 Parties … accounting in total for at least an estimated 55 per cent” is a conjunction: a large number of small emitters alone does not satisfy it, and a small number of large emitters alone does not satisfy it.
- **No reservations.** Article 27 prohibits reservations, so no instrument can qualify or vary the threshold.
- **Withdrawals after entry into force do not reverse it.** Article 21 contains no reverse-threshold. The United States withdrawal that took effect on 27 January 2026 (per the UNTC note) does not alter the fact or the date of entry into force, and the note should not suggest otherwise.

## 7. Date arithmetic (how to compute the interval)

**Rule.** Take the date on which the last deposit needed to satisfy both conditions is made (or, for a later participant, the date of its own deposit). Do **not** count that date. The following day is day 1; the Agreement enters into force on day 30. Equivalently: entry-into-force date = trigger date + 30 calendar days. This is “the thirtieth day after the date”, not “within 30 days” and not “after 30 days have elapsed”.

**Worked checks (all consistent with the 30-day interval stated above):**

| Trigger date | Day 1 | Day 30 = entry into force |
|---|---|---|
| 5 Oct 2016 (conditions fulfilled) | 6 Oct 2016 | **4 Nov 2016** — matches the UNTC record |
| 21 Nov 2026 (deposit) | 22 Nov 2026 | 21 Dec 2026 |
| 1 Dec 2026 | 2 Dec 2026 | 31 Dec 2026 |
| 20 Dec 2026 | 21 Dec 2026 | 19 Jan 2027 (31 Dec = day 11) |
| 1 Feb 2028 (leap year) | 2 Feb 2028 | 2 Mar 2028 (29 Feb = day 28) |

The first row is the decisive control: the UNTC records entry into force on 4 November 2016 in accordance with Article 21(1), and 5 October 2016 + 30 days = 4 November 2016 under the rule above. Any arithmetic convention that produces a different date for that pair is the wrong convention.

## 8. Verification checklist before the note is signed off

1. Open the certified true copy (UNTS vol. 3156, p. 79) or the UNFCCC secretariat English text and confirm Article 21(1) contains exactly three numbers: **55**, **55 per cent**, **thirtieth day**. No other number appears in that paragraph.
2. Confirm Article 21(2)'s definition and the 12 December 2015 cut-off are reproduced or correctly paraphrased.
3. Confirm Article 21(3) (later depositors, 30 days) is used wherever the note addresses a specific Party's date of entry into force.
4. Confirm Article 21(4) (REIO non-addition) is stated wherever the count of 55 is explained.
5. Confirm the historical sentence uses **4 November 2016**, not 5 October 2016 (the latter is the date the conditions were met, not the entry-into-force date).
6. Run the §4.6 searches; no residual “fiftieth” or “ninetieth” outside an express comparison.
7. Confirm the citation names the UNTS volume/page and registration number, and states the currency of the status record.

## 9. Scope boundaries and residual risks

- **Scope.** Per the instruction, this memo covers the Agreement's **original** entry-into-force provision only. The amendment and annex provisions (Articles 22–23) use different procedures and are **not** stated here, because they are outside the grounded material for this request; if the note needs them, check them separately against the same publication.
- **No analogy from the Convention.** The 90-day rule must not be imported by analogy, and the 50-instrument count must not be retained as a “minimum”. The Agreement's rule is self-contained.
- **Risk of a stale snapshot.** The two-day gap between the requested date (21 Nov 2026) and the consultation date (23 Nov 2026) is disclosed in §3; it does not affect any value. A date-stamped archive copy removes the point entirely.
- **Risk of a mis-citation.** The frequently cited UNFCCC PDF is the secretariat's text; the legally authoritative version is the certified true copy registered as No. 54113. Cite both, with the UNTS reference leading.

question: Y23
answer:
ANSWER

12 nautical miles.

The contiguous zone can extend 12 nautical miles farther from the baselines than the territorial sea.

LEGAL BASIS (UNCLOS, Part II)

- Article 3 (Breadth of the territorial sea): "Every State has the right to establish the breadth of its territorial sea up to a limit not exceeding 12 nautical miles, measured from baselines determined in accordance with this Convention."
- Article 4 (Outer limit of the territorial sea): the outer limit is the line every point of which is at a distance from the nearest point of the baseline equal to the breadth of the territorial sea.
- Article 33(2) (Contiguous zone): "The contiguous zone may not extend beyond 24 nautical miles from the baselines from which the breadth of the territorial sea is measured."

DERIVATION

Let B be the baseline system. Under the request's stipulation both zones are measured from the same B and both are taken at their UNCLOS maxima.

  Territorial sea outer limit   T = 12 nm from B   (Art. 3 maximum)
  Contiguous zone outer limit    C = 24 nm from B   (Art. 33(2) maximum)
  Difference                     C − T = 24 − 12 = 12 nm

So the contiguous zone reaches 12 nm beyond the outer edge of the territorial sea. Equivalently, the contiguous zone spans the band from 0 to 24 nm from the baselines, of which the inner 0–12 nm coincides with the territorial sea and the outer 12–24 nm is the additional band that exists only by virtue of the contiguous-zone regime.

CHECK AGAINST THE STATED LIMITS

  - 12 nm does not exceed the Art. 3 territorial-sea cap (12 nm): satisfied.
  - 24 nm does not exceed the Art. 33(2) contiguous-zone cap (24 nm): satisfied.
  - The derived additional band (12–24 nm) lies entirely outside the territorial sea and entirely within the Art. 33(2) ceiling: satisfied.
  - Both measurements use one and the same baseline system, as the request requires: satisfied.

QUALIFICATIONS A MARITIME LAWYER WOULD FLAG (they do not change the figure)

1. The 12 nm figure is the maximum differential, arising only because the request fixes both zones at their maxima. If a State claims a territorial sea narrower than 12 nm (e.g., 3 nm), the contiguous zone may still run to 24 nm from the same baselines, and the differential becomes 24 − (that breadth). The 12 nm answer is therefore conditional on the stipulated maximum territorial sea.
2. The contiguous zone is not 'territorial sea plus 12 nm of sovereignty.' Under Art. 33(1) the coastal State may exercise there only the control necessary to prevent and punish infringement of its customs, fiscal, immigration or sanitary laws and regulations committed within its territory or territorial sea. The inner 12 nm of the contiguous zone is already territorial sea, where the coastal State enjoys full sovereignty (Art. 2), so the practically meaningful 'extra' area is the outer 12 nm band.
3. Article 33 does not require a State to claim a contiguous zone at all, and a State may claim less than 24 nm; 24 nm is a ceiling, not an entitlement that operates automatically.
4. The measurement is from the same baselines used for the territorial sea — normal baselines (Art. 5), straight baselines (Art. 7), or, for an archipelagic State, archipelagic baselines (Art. 47). The identity of the baseline system does not alter the arithmetic; it only fixes where the 12 nm and 24 nm lines fall geographically.
5. Art. 4 defines the territorial sea's outer limit as a line every point of which is equidistant (by the stated breadth) from the nearest baseline point; the Art. 33(2) ceiling is expressed the same way ('from the baselines'), so the two limits are parallel constructions and the subtraction is dimensionally sound.

RESULT

Ask 3: 12 (nautical miles).
Asks 1, 2 and 4 are constraints/format instructions, not value or verdict asks; they are satisfied by the analysis above (UNCLOS as the governing instrument, both zones at their maxima from the same baselines, answer expressed in nautical miles).

question: Y24
answer:
LEGAL OPINION — Availability of the UNCLOS Article 10 bay closing-line rule to a bay with a 30 nm entrance

1. QUESTION PRESENTED
Whether, under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, a bay whose natural entrance points are 30 nautical miles apart (measured between the low-water marks) may have a closing line drawn between those low-water marks so as to make the enclosed waters internal waters; and, if not on those facts, what the maximum entrance-point distance for that rule is.

2. SHORT ANSWERS
(1) No. The rule the reviewer invokes is not available to a bay with a 30 nm entrance. The passage makes the closing line conditional on the entrance distance NOT EXCEEDING 24 nautical miles; 30 nm exceeds 24 nm, so the condition fails and the closing line between the natural entrance points cannot be drawn under that rule.
(2) 24 nautical miles, measured between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points.

3. GOVERNING TEXT
The controlling provision is Article 10 of UNCLOS. The operative paragraphs, as they appear verbatim in the sourced text (identical across the UN Part II page, the DOALOS compendium, the UN Audiovisual Library treaty text, and the UK reproduction at SI 2014/1353 Sch. 1):

  Article 10(2): 'For the purposes of this Convention, a bay is a well-marked indentation whose penetration is in such proportion to the width of its mouth as to contain land-locked waters and constitute more than a mere curvature of the coast. An indentation shall not, however, be regarded as a bay unless its area is as large as, or larger than, that of the semi-circle whose diameter is a line drawn across the mouth of that indentation.'

  Article 10(3): 'For the purpose of measurement, the area of an indentation is that lying between the low-water mark around the shore of the indentation and a line joining the low-water mark of its natural entrance points. Where, because of the presence of islands, an indentation has more than one mouth, the semi-circle shall be drawn on a line as long as the sum total of the lengths of the lines across the different mouths. Islands within an indentation shall be included as if they were part of the water area of the indentation.'

  Article 10(4): 'If the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of a bay does not exceed 24 nautical miles, a closing line may be drawn between these two low-water marks, and the waters enclosed thereby shall be considered as internal waters.'

  Article 10(5): 'Where the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points of a bay exceeds 24 nautical miles, a straight baseline of 24 nautical miles shall be drawn within the bay in such a manner as to enclose the maximum area of water that is possible with a line of that length.'

  Article 10(6) (as reproduced in the UN Audiovisual Library text and the UNFSA/unclos_e.pdf text): 'The foregoing provisions do not apply to so-called "historic" bays, ...'

4. ANALYSIS
4.1 The rule is stated as a conditional. Article 10(4) is framed as 'If the distance ... does not exceed 24 nautical miles, a closing line may be drawn.' The permission ('may be drawn') is not free-standing; it exists only inside the stated condition. Outside the condition the permission does not exist. This is the ordinary reading of a conditional grant, and the passage itself supplies the alternative rule for the outside case in paragraph 5.

4.2 The measurement basis is the same one the reviewer used. Article 10(4) measures 'the distance between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points.' The reviewer's 30 nm figure is, on the stated assumption, measured the same way. There is therefore no measurement discrepancy to argue about: the figure is 30 nm on the convention's own basis, and 30 > 24.

4.3 The consequence of the 30 nm figure. Because the entrance exceeds 24 nm, Article 10(4) is inapplicable and Article 10(5) governs: 'a straight baseline of 24 nautical miles shall be drawn within the bay in such a manner as to enclose the maximum area of water that is possible with a line of that length.' The practical result is the opposite of what the reviewer asserts: (a) the closing line is drawn INSIDE the bay, not between the natural entrance points; (b) it is capped at 24 nm; (c) the waters enclosed by that inner line are internal waters, but the waters between that line and the natural entrance points are not enclosed as internal waters — they remain territorial sea (subject to the ordinary regime, including innocent passage), because the baseline there is the low-water line and the belt seaward of it is territorial sea under Articles 3 and 4.

4.4 Why the reviewer's proposition fails. It asserts an unconditional entitlement ('a bay with natural entrance points 30 nautical miles apart may have a closing line drawn between those low-water marks, making the enclosed waters internal waters') that the passage does not contain. The passage contains that entitlement only up to 24 nm. The reviewer has taken the correct rule and applied it past its stated ceiling.

4.5 Likely source of the error — flagged, not relied on. 24 nm is a number that appears in the law of the sea in more than one place (for example, the outer limit of the contiguous zone is 24 nm from the baselines, and the territorial sea breadth is up to 12 nm under Article 3). It is possible the reviewer has carried a 24 nm figure across from a different rule, or has assumed the bay closing line follows the outer territorial-sea geometry rather than the special bay rule. Nothing in the passage supports extending the bay closing line beyond 24 nm. On the facts given, the error is simply that 30 exceeds 24.

4.6 Conditions that sit alongside Article 10(4) — noted, and assumed not to change the outcome. Even for a bay whose entrance does NOT exceed 24 nm, the closing line is available only if: (a) the coasts of the bay belong to a single State (Art. 10(1)); (b) the indentation satisfies the definition and the semicircle-area test in Art. 10(2)–(3); and (c) the bay is not a 'historic' bay, to which the foregoing provisions do not apply (Art. 10(6)). These conditions are cumulative with the 24 nm ceiling and can only further restrict, never expand, the availability of the rule. Because the 30 nm entrance already defeats Article 10(4) on its own, the request's assumption that these other conditions do not alter the outcome is safe: the answer would be 'No' regardless of how they were resolved.

4.7 Scope note. This opinion addresses only the availability of the Article 10 closing-line rule. It does not address whether the waters in question could be enclosed as internal waters on some other basis (for example a historic title under Art. 10(6), straight baselines under Art. 7 where the geography is genuinely exceptional, or a river mouth under Art. 9). Those are separate routes requiring separate facts; none of them is the rule the reviewer stated, and none is established by the facts given.

5. CONCLUSIONS
(1) Is the rule available under the passage for a bay with natural entrance points 30 nm apart? No. Article 10(4)'s closing-line rule is conditional on the entrance distance not exceeding 24 nm; at 30 nm the condition is not met, and Article 10(5) instead requires a 24 nm straight baseline drawn within the bay enclosing the maximum area.
(2) Maximum entrance-point distance for the rule: 24 nautical miles, measured between the low-water marks of the natural entrance points (Art. 10(4)).

question: Y25
answer:
Scope and source

This answers the question against Article II of the 1972 Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, the provision that establishes absolute liability for damage caused by a space object on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight. The quoted text was retrieved from the public UNOOSA and FAA versions of the Convention.

Ask 1 — Does the passage stating absolute liability give a monetary cap?

No. Article II contains no monetary cap. It states no ceiling, no fixed sum, no formula, no maximum amount, and no cross-reference to a monetary limit. The provision is a single sentence establishing liability and the obligation to pay compensation; it does not quantify compensation.

Ask 2 — What the passage does say about liability

Article II states:

"A launching State shall be absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight."

(One UNOOSA rendering reads "to aircraft flight"; the FAA and Lovdata texts read "to aircraft in flight." The difference is a textual/typographical variance and does not affect the answer.)

The passage therefore says, in substance:

1. The liable party is a "launching State."
2. The standard of liability is "absolutely liable" — i.e., liability is not conditioned on fault in the text of Article II.
3. The obligation is "to pay compensation."
4. The damage must be "caused by its space object."
5. The damage must occur "on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight."

What the passage does not say

Article II does not state a monetary cap; it does not state any monetary amount; it does not prescribe a formula for calculating compensation; it does not set a maximum recoverable sum; and it does not refer to another provision that sets a cap. Absolute liability under Article II is a standard of liability, not a limitation on the amount of compensation.

This answer is confined to the absolute-liability passage. It does not opine on whether any other provision of the Convention, outside Article II, addresses the measure or limits of compensation; that would require a separate review of the full text. For the auditor's question as framed, the operative answer is: no monetary cap appears in Article II, and Article II says only that the launching State is absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight.

question: Y26
answer:
IDENTIFICATION OF THE INSTRUMENT AND PROVISION

The supplied UN treaty text is the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (Vienna, 23 May 1969), Part V, Section 3 ('Termination and Suspension of the Operation of Treaties'), Article 56, headed 'Denunciation of or withdrawal from a treaty containing no provision regarding termination, denunciation or withdrawal'. The operative text, as it appears in the supplied document, reads:

  'Article 56
   Denunciation of or withdrawal from a treaty containing no
   provision regarding termination, denunciation or withdrawal
   1. A treaty which contains no provision regarding its termination and which does not provide for denunciation or withdrawal is not subject to denunciation or withdrawal unless:
   (a) it is established that the parties intended to admit the possibility of denunciation or withdrawal; or
   (b) a right of denunciation or withdrawal may be implied by the nature of the treaty.
   2. A party shall give not less than twelve months' notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under paragraph 1.'

ANSWER

Minimum notice period: twelve (12) months. Unit: months.

Ground: Article 56, paragraph 2, second sentence — 'not less than twelve months' notice'. Because the text says 'not less than', twelve months is a floor: a notice shorter than twelve months does not satisfy Article 56(2); a longer notice does.

WHY 'PARAGRAPH 1' POINTS HERE

1. The request's phrase 'under paragraph 1' is not a free-floating description: it is the exact cross-reference written into Article 56(2) ('... from a treaty under paragraph 1'). No other denunciation/withdrawal provision in the Convention carries that formulation.
2. Paragraph 1 itself contains no period. It supplies only the conditions under which a treaty that is silent on termination, denunciation and withdrawal may nonetheless be denounced (intention of the parties, or implication from the nature of the treaty). The notice requirement is deliberately placed in paragraph 2, which is why a reader who stops at paragraph 1 will find no figure and must read on to paragraph 2.
3. Corroboration inside the supplied corpus:
   - ILC Commentary to draft article 53 (1966), paragraph (6): '... it preferred in paragraph 2 to specify that not less than twelve months' notice must be given of an intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under the present article.'
   - Draft article 53(2), 1966: 'A party shall give not less than twelve months' notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under paragraph 1 of this article.'
   - 1979 redraft (A/CN.4/L.300), Article 56(2): 'A party shall give not less than twelve months notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty under paragraph 1.'
   - UN publication on the fulfilment of Charter obligations: 'A party must give at least 12 months' notice of its intention to denounce or withdraw from a treaty (see article 56 of the Vienna Convention, 1969).'
All four independent renderings in the supplied material give the same figure: twelve months.

HOW TO APPLY IT (operational rule)

- Start the clock at the date the notice of intention to denounce or withdraw is given (received by the counterparty/depositary as the treaty or the applicable procedural articles require).
- The earliest date on which the denunciation or withdrawal may take effect is that date plus twelve months. Notice given on day D supports an effective date no earlier than D + 12 months.
- Do not confuse the notice period with the eligibility gate. Article 56 does not require any period of membership before notice may be given; the three-year and four-year gates that appear elsewhere in the supplied material (e.g. the chemical-weapons-type and ozone-layer-type clauses quoted in the UN publication) belong to other conventions and do not modify Article 56.
- The figure is a default, not a mandatory term of every treaty: Article 56 applies only where the treaty is silent. Where the treaty itself fixes a period (six months, one year, ninety days, etc. — all of which appear in the supplied material for other instruments), that treaty provision prevails, and Article 56(2)'s twelve months is displaced.

CAVEATS DISCLOSED RATHER THAN HIDDEN

- The file does not name the convention. The identification above rests on the fact that the supplied text is the Vienna Convention text and that the 'paragraph 1' cross-reference is unique to Article 56(2) within it. If the underlying file were in truth a different instrument (e.g. one of the conventions quoted in the same corpus providing six months or one year), the answer would change; on the text supplied, it is twelve months.
- The question asks for the minimum, which the text itself fixes as a floor ('not less than'); it is not a maximum and no upper bound is imposed by Article 56(2).
- Article 56(2) governs denunciation and withdrawal indifferently; the text uses the two verbs in the same sentence, so no separate figure applies to one but not the other.

CONCLUSION

Under paragraph 1 of the relevant article — Article 56 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, 1969 — the minimum notice a party must give of its intention to denounce or withdraw is twelve months.

question: Y27
answer:
The relevant instrument is the Optional Protocol to the Vienna Convention on Consular Relations concerning the Compulsory Settlement of Disputes (Vienna, 24 April 1963).

Article III(1) provides: "Within the same period of two months, the parties may agree to adopt a conciliation procedure before resorting to the International Court of Justice." The "same period of two months" is the period stated in Article II, i.e. two months after one party has notified its opinion to the other that a dispute exists.

Article III(2) provides: "The conciliation commission shall, unless the parties otherwise agree, make its recommendations within five months after its appointment."

The requested calculation is arithmetic only:

2 months (period for agreeing to adopt a conciliation procedure) + 5 months (period after the commission's appointment for it to make recommendations) = 7 months.

The two periods are distinct: the first is a window for the parties to agree to a conciliation procedure; the second is the default period for the conciliation commission's recommendations after its appointment. The resulting 7 months is not a composite or continuous deadline measured from notification of the dispute, and it should not be treated as one. The qualification "unless the parties otherwise agree" in Article III(2) does not alter the stated five-month figure for purposes of this sum.
