question: Y29
answer:
RFC 7519 — RULE FOR DUPLICATE CLAIM NAMES IN A JWT CLAIMS SET

1. VERBATIM NORMATIVE TEXT

Source: RFC 7519 (JSON Web Token (JWT)), May 2015, Section 4 ("JWT Claims"), first paragraph. The paragraph appears immediately after the sentence defining the Claims Set as a JSON object and immediately before "The set of claims that a JWT must contain to be considered valid is context dependent...".

The text, exactly as it appears in the RFC:

    The JWT Claims Set represents a JSON object whose members are the
    claims conveyed by the JWT.  The Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set
    MUST be unique; JWT parsers MUST either reject JWTs with duplicate
    Claim Names or use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last
    duplicate member name, as specified in Section 15.12 ("The JSON
    Object") of ECMAScript 5.1 [ECMAScript].

That is the answer. Everything below is decomposition, scope, and engineering consequence.

2. NORMATIVE DECOMPOSITION

The paragraph contains three distinct obligations, on three distinct actors:

  O1. Producers / the data model — "The Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set MUST be unique." This is a requirement on the Claims Set itself: a conforming JWT Claims Set never contains the same Claim Name twice. A token with duplicate Claim Names is a non-conforming Claims Set.

  O2. Parsers, option A — "JWT parsers MUST either reject JWTs with duplicate Claim Names ...". A parser satisfies the rule by detecting duplication and refusing the token.

  O3. Parsers, option B — "... or use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last duplicate member name, as specified in Section 15.12 ("The JSON Object") of ECMAScript 5.1 [ECMAScript]." A parser satisfies the rule by collapsing duplicates deterministically to the last occurrence in document order.

O2 and O3 are alternatives joined by "either ... or"; the RFC mandates that a parser do one of them. It does not mandate which. A parser that keeps the FIRST occurrence, that keeps a nondeterministic occurrence, that merges values, or that silently accepts duplicates and leaves the resolution to whichever JSON library is linked, violates the MUST.

3. SCOPE OF THE RULE

  - It lives in Section 4, not Section 4.1. It therefore applies to all Claim Names, not just the Registered Claim Names (iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti). It applies equally to Public Claim Names (Section 4.2) and Private Claim Names (Section 4.3). A duplicate private claim name is as much a violation as a duplicate "iss".
  - It applies to the JWT Claims Set regardless of how the JWT is represented. Per Section 3, the Claims Set is the JWS Payload when the JWT is a JWS, and the JWE plaintext when the JWT is a JWE. The rule attaches to the Claims Set, so it binds in both representations and in nested JWS/JWE constructions.
  - It is about member names of the Claims Set object (the top-level members). A JSON object nested inside a claim value that happens to contain duplicate names is not a duplicate "Claim Name" under this paragraph; the RFC's sentence is scoped to "the Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set".
  - Duplicate means the same member name string. JSON member names are compared as strings; "iss" and "ISS" are different names, and neither is a duplicate of the other.
  - Out of scope of this paragraph: the JOSE Header. The quoted rule speaks only of the JWT Claims Set. Do not cite RFC 7519 Section 4 as authority for duplicate-parameter handling in the protected/unprotected header; that is a different question with a different source.

4. WHAT THE RFC DOES NOT SAY (frequently mis-cited)

  - It does not require rejection. Rejection is one of two permitted behaviours.
  - It does not specify an error code, error type, or HTTP status for rejection. "Reject" is left unqualified; the application layer chooses the failure surface.
  - It does not say the whole JWT is invalid versus just the duplicated claim. Under O2 the token is rejected; under O3 the token is accepted with the last value. There is no third "drop the claim and continue" option in the text.
  - It does not define "lexically last" as alphabetically greatest. In ECMAScript 5.1 Section 15.12 the operative notion is the last occurrence in the text of the object. "Lexically last" here means last in lexical (document) order. Implementations that sort names or compare strings to pick a winner are not implementing option B.
  - It does not say the two options are equally safe. See Section 6.

5. IMPLEMENTATION PROCEDURE

Recommended default for new code: option A (strict rejection). It is the only option that is identical across every component in a pipeline, so it cannot be exploited by a parser-differential attack.

5.1 Strict parser (option A), Python 3, enforcing the rule at the Claims Set level only:

    import json

    class DuplicateClaimName(ValueError):
        """RFC 7519 Section 4: Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set MUST be unique."""
        def __init__(self, name):
            super().__init__(f"duplicate Claim Name in JWT Claims Set: {name!r}")
            self.name = name

    class _Members(list):
        """Marker so we can tell a JSON object from a JSON array."""
        pass

    def _collect(pairs):
        return _Members(pairs)   # preserves order AND duplicates

    def parse_claims_strict(payload: bytes) -> dict:
        top = json.loads(payload.decode("utf-8"), object_pairs_hook=_collect)
        if not isinstance(top, _Members):
            raise ValueError("JWT Claims Set must be a JSON object")
        claims = {}
        for name, value in top:
            if name in claims:
                raise DuplicateClaimName(name)   # O2: reject
            claims[name] = value
        return _normalize(claims)

    def _normalize(node):
        # Nested objects were also captured as _Members; convert them to dicts
        # (last-wins inside nested values is NOT governed by RFC 7519 Section 4).
        if isinstance(node, _Members):
            out = {}
            for k, v in node:
                out[k] = _normalize(v)
            return out
        if isinstance(node, list):
            return [_normalize(v) for v in node]
        return node

    Note on why object_pairs_hook is required: a plain json.loads silently applies last-wins to every object and destroys the evidence that a duplicate existed. Duplicate detection is impossible after a normal parse. The same is true of most default JSON bindings in other languages (JavaScript JSON.parse, Go encoding/json into map, Java Jackson into Map, .NET System.Text.Json into Dictionary) — each silently keeps one value, and not always the same one.

5.2 Option B parser (last-in-document-order wins), for interop with peers that demand it:

    def parse_claims_last_wins(payload: bytes) -> dict:
        top = json.loads(payload.decode("utf-8"), object_pairs_hook=_collect)
        if not isinstance(top, _Members):
            raise ValueError("JWT Claims Set must be a JSON object")
        claims = {}
        for name, value in top:
            claims[name] = value      # later occurrence overwrites earlier one
        return _normalize(claims)

    Correctness note: this satisfies O3 because Python dict assignment in iteration order keeps the final occurrence in document order. It would NOT satisfy O3 if the pairs were sorted first, or if "last" were taken to mean max(name).

5.3 Placement in the validation pipeline. Run the duplicate check on the decoded Claims Set bytes BEFORE any claim is consumed for authorization decisions, and before signature verification is relied upon for trust. Ordering matters: signature verification proves the bytes were signed, not that the Claims Set was well-formed. A token with a valid signature over a Claims Set containing two "sub" members is a validly-signed non-conforming JWT, and must still be rejected under option A.

6. SECURITY RATIONALE FOR PREFERRING OPTION A

Option B is legal but is the classic parser-differential hazard: if the JWT passes through two components that both implement option B differently — or one that implements option A and one that implements B — the value that the authorization layer sees may not be the value that the issuer intended or that the audit log records. A token carrying two "sub" or two "aud" members can be made to authenticate as one principal at the gateway and be logged as another. Because RFC 7519 permits rejection outright, rejecting costs nothing in conformance and eliminates the class. Deployments that must accept option B should confine duplicate resolution to a single trusted library and never re-serialize/re-parse the Claims Set downstream.

7. TEST VECTORS

Each payload below is the raw JSON to be base64url-encoded into the JWS/JWE payload segment (encoding omitted deliberately; the JSON is the test input).

  T1  {"iss":"https://as.example","sub":"alice","aud":"api"}
      No duplicates. Option A: accept. Option B: accept.

  T2  {"iss":"https://as.example","sub":"alice","sub":"admin"}
      Duplicate "sub". Option A: reject with DuplicateClaimName('sub'). Option B: accept with sub == "admin".

  T3  {"iss":"https://as.example","sub":"admin","sub":"alice"}
      Duplicate "sub", reversed order. Option A: reject. Option B: accept with sub == "alice". T2 and T3 together prove the implementation is order-sensitive, as option B requires.

  T4  {"aud":"api","exp":1700000000,"aud":"api"}
      Duplicate with identical values. Still a duplicate Claim Name; the rule is about names, not values. Option A: reject. Option B: accept.

  T5  {"iss":"a","ISS":"b"}
      Not a duplicate — names differ in case. Option A: accept. Option B: accept.

  T6  {"sub":"alice","meta":{"k":1,"k":2}}
      Duplicate inside a nested value, not at the Claims Set level. Option A: accept the Claims Set (nested resolution is application policy, outside RFC 7519 Section 4). Option B: accept.

  T7  {"sub":"alice","sub":"admin","iss":"https://as.example","sub":"root"}
      Triple duplicate. Option A: reject. Option B: accept with sub == "root" (last in document order, not max string).

  T8  A Claims Set that is a JSON array or scalar, e.g. ["alice"]
      Not an object, therefore not a valid Claims Set. Reject before duplicate analysis.

8. CONFORMANCE CHECKLIST

  [ ] Duplicate detection runs on the raw decoded Claims Set bytes, not on an already-parsed map.
  [ ] The chosen behaviour is exactly one of: reject, or last-in-document-order-wins. Never first-wins, never nondeterministic.
  [ ] Detection is applied to all Claim Name classes, not only Registered Claim Names.
  [ ] Detection is applied at the Claims Set top level; nested-object duplicate policy is documented separately.
  [ ] Claim Name comparison is exact string comparison, case-sensitive.
  [ ] The check executes before any claim value influences authorization or audit output.
  [ ] The rejection path produces a distinguishable, logged error (name of the offending claim) rather than a generic parse failure.
  [ ] The behaviour is identical in every component that parses the token in the request path.

9. ONE-SENTENCE RESTATEMENT FOR CITATION

RFC 7519 Section 4 requires Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set to be unique, and requires JWT parsers either to reject JWTs with duplicate Claim Names or to use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last duplicate member name, per ECMAScript 5.1 Section 15.12.

question: Y30
answer:
ANSWER

RFC 7519 (JWT), Section 8 ("Implementation Requirements"), states normatively that exactly two of the signature/MAC algorithm identifiers registered by JSON Web Algorithms (JWA = RFC 7518) MUST be implemented by a conforming JWT implementation:

  1. HS256 — HMAC using SHA-256 (a MAC algorithm, RFC 7518 §3.2)
  2. none  — the unsecured JWS mode, i.e. no signature/MAC at all (RFC 7515 §4.1.1 / Appendix A.5)

Everything else in the JWS signature/MAC family is at most RECOMMENDED or OPTIONAL.

VERBATIM SOURCE (RFC 7519 §8, fetched from rfc-editor.org):

  "Of the signature and MAC algorithms specified in JSON Web Algorithms
   [JWA], only HMAC SHA-256 (\"HS256\") and \"none\" MUST be implemented by
   conforming JWT implementations.  It is RECOMMENDED that
   implementations also support RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 with the SHA-256 hash
   algorithm (\"RS256\") and ECDSA using the P-256 curve and the SHA-256
   hash algorithm (\"ES256\").  Support for other algorithms and key sizes
   is OPTIONAL."

Corroborating registry entry (RFC 7518 §7.1.2, IANA "JSON Web Signature and Encryption Algorithms"): Algorithm Name "HS256", Description "HMAC using SHA-256", Usage Location(s) "alg", JOSE Implementation Requirements: **Required**. HS384 and HS512 are listed as **Optional** in the same registry.

REQUIREMENT LEVELS FOR THE FULL JWS SIGNATURE/MAC SET (per RFC 7519 §8)

  | alg    | Algorithm                                  | RFC 7519 §8 level |
  |--------|--------------------------------------------|-------------------|
  | HS256  | HMAC using SHA-256                         | MUST              |
  | none   | No digital signature or MAC                | MUST              |
  | RS256  | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-256             | RECOMMENDED       |
  | ES256  | ECDSA using P-256 curve and SHA-256        | RECOMMENDED       |
  | HS384  | HMAC using SHA-384                         | OPTIONAL          |
  | HS512  | HMAC using SHA-512                         | OPTIONAL          |
  | RS384  | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-384             | OPTIONAL          |
  | RS512  | RSASSA-PKCS1-v1_5 using SHA-512             | OPTIONAL          |
  | ES384  | ECDSA using P-384 curve and SHA-384        | OPTIONAL          |
  | ES512  | ECDSA using P-521 curve and SHA-512        | OPTIONAL          |
  | PS256  | RSASSA-PSS using SHA-256 and MGF1(SHA-256)  | OPTIONAL          |
  | PS384  | RSASSA-PSS using SHA-384 and MGF1(SHA-384)  | OPTIONAL          |
  | PS512  | RSASSA-PSS using SHA-512 and MGF1(SHA-512)  | OPTIONAL          |

("Support for other algorithms and key sizes is OPTIONAL" is the catch-all clause covering every row not marked MUST/RECOMMENDED.)

INTERPRETATION NOTES AN IMPLEMENTER MUST GET RIGHT

1. "MUST" is a two-element set, and one element is the absence of a signature. The only *cryptographic* algorithm a conforming JWT implementation is required to implement is HS256. "none" is the unsecured JWS variant; implementing it means being able to parse/produce a JWS with `"alg":"none"` and an empty signature segment. Consequently a conforming implementation is NOT required to implement any public-key digital signature algorithm — RS256 and ES256 are RECOMMENDED, not MUST.

2. "none" MUST be implemented ≠ "none" may be accepted. RFC 7519 §8 is an implementation-capability requirement. Acceptance is a separate policy decision: a JWT consumer must not treat `"alg":"none"` as valid unless the application has explicitly opted in to unsecured JWTs; otherwise it is an algorithm-confusion / signature-stripping vulnerability. Implementing "none" and then rejecting it at the verification boundary is compliant.

3. HS256 carries a key-size constraint from JWA (RFC 7518 §3.2): "A key of the same size as the hash output (e.g., 256 bits for 'HS256') or larger MUST be used with this algorithm." So an HS256 implementation that accepts a shared secret shorter than 256 bits is not conformant with JWA even though it implements the algorithm identifier. RFC 7518's rationale cites NIST SP 800-107 §5.3.4: effective security strength is the minimum of the key's strength and twice the internal hash size.

4. Scope. This answer is scoped to signature and MAC algorithms (`alg` values used with JWS/JWT). The same RFC 7519 §8 paragraph separately mandates, only if encryption is offered at all, RSA1_5, A128KW, A256KW, A128CBC-HS256 and A256CBC-HS512 — that is a JWE requirement and is not part of the answer to this ask.

5. Normative references. RFC 7519 does not itself define algorithms; it defers to JWA (RFC 7518) and JWS (RFC 7515). The MUST statement above lives in RFC 7519 §8; the algorithm definitions and the "Required" registry marking for HS256 live in RFC 7518 §3.2 and §7.1.2 respectively.

6. Currency caveat. The RFC Editor's info page for RFC 7518 carries the banner "This RFC was updated, see RFC 9864." I have not retrieved or verified the text of RFC 9864, so I do not characterize its contents here. The answer above states RFC 7519 §8 / RFC 7518 as published (May 2015). Before relying on this for a security review, check RFC 9864 (and the RFC 7519 errata) for any change affecting the standing of "none" — the likely area of impact — while noting that HS256's status is not in question in any source I have seen.

SHORT FORM FOR A SPEC/TEST-MATRIX LINE

  Required by RFC 7519 §8 for conforming JWT implementations:
    HS256 (HMAC-SHA-256) — MUST
    none (unsecured JWS) — MUST
  Recommended: RS256, ES256
  All others (HS384, HS512, RS384, RS512, ES384, ES512, PS256, PS384, PS512, and any non-registered alg): OPTIONAL

question: Y31
answer:
RFC 7515 (JSON Web Signature, JWS), Section 7.1 'JWS Compact Serialization', states normatively:

  'Only one signature/MAC is supported by the JWS Compact Serialization and it provides no syntax to represent a JWS Unprotected Header value.'

Answers

1. Number of signatures or MACs supported by the JWS Compact Serialization: 1 (exactly one signature or MAC value).

2. Header syntax it lacks: the JWS Unprotected Header — i.e., there is no syntax in the Compact Serialization to represent an unprotected header. The Compact Serialization carries only the JWS Protected Header, so the JOSE Header is identical to the JWS Protected Header.

Supporting normative text

- Section 3.1 (JWS Compact Serialization Overview): 'In the JWS Compact Serialization, no JWS Unprotected Header is used. In this case, the JOSE Header and the JWS Protected Header are the same.' The serialization is exactly:

    BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header)) || '.' ||
    BASE64URL(JWS Payload) || '.' ||
    BASE64URL(JWS Signature)

  There is one header segment and one signature segment; the three period-delimited segments admit no second signature and no second header.

- Section 7.1: 'Only one signature/MAC is supported by the JWS Compact Serialization and it provides no syntax to represent a JWS Unprotected Header value.'

Contrast with the JWS JSON Serialization (why the missing syntax matters)

- Section 7.2 defines the JWS JSON Serialization in two forms: the general syntax, which can secure content 'with more than one digital signature and/or MAC operation' via the top-level 'signatures' array, and the flattened syntax for the single signature/MAC case.
- Section 7.2.1 defines the per-signature members 'protected' (BASE64URL(UTF8(JWS Protected Header)), integrity protected) and 'header' (the JWS Unprotected Header as an unencoded JSON object, not integrity protected). The Compact Serialization has no equivalent of the 'header' member and no equivalent of the 'signatures' array.

Practical consequence for implementers

A Compact-serialized JWS is a single-signature/single-MAC, single-header artifact. Any requirement for multiple signatures/MACs (e.g., multi-party signing, algorithm migration with dual signatures, or attaching non-integrity-protected header parameters) cannot be expressed in the Compact Serialization and must use the JWS JSON Serialization (general syntax). A parser for the Compact Serialization should reject input with more than two '.' separators (i.e., anything other than exactly three segments), and must not expect an unprotected header segment.
